questions.q: Define the Tyndall effect and state the size range of particles that exhibit it.
questions.a: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles (1 nm – 1000 nm) making the light path visible. A wrong answer (e.g., "scattering by any particles" or "size >1000 nm") reveals the student confuses colloids with suspensions or does not know the critical size criterion linking particle dimensions to light wavelength.

questions.q: Why does a true solution of copper sulphate not show the Tyndall effect, while a colloidal solution of starch does? Explain using particle size and light wavelength.
questions.a: CuSO₄ solution has ions/molecules <1 nm, much smaller than visible light wavelength (400-700 nm), so no scattering occurs. Starch colloid has particles 1-1000 nm, comparable to light wavelength, causing strong scattering. A wrong answer (e.g., "starch is coloured" or "CuSO₄ is transparent") shows the student relies on appearance rather than the size-wavelength relationship.

questions.q: A student shines a laser pointer through three beakers: (A) salt water, (B) milk diluted 1:100, (C) muddy water. In which beaker(s) will the beam be visible? Justify your answer for each.
questions.a: Beam visible only in (B) milk (colloid, 1-1000 nm fat/protein particles scatter light). Not visible in (A) salt water (true solution, ions <1 nm). Not visible in (C) muddy water (suspension, particles >1000 nm settle quickly and block light rather than scatter). A wrong answer identifying (C) shows confusion between suspension and colloid; identifying (A) shows misunderstanding of true solutions.

questions.q: Compare the Tyndall effect observed in a colloid with the scattering of sunlight by atmospheric molecules (Rayleigh scattering). How are the particle sizes and scattering intensity different?
questions.a: Rayleigh scattering: particles (N₂, O₂ molecules) ~0.3 nm, much smaller than wavelength, scattering intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴ (blue sky). Tyndall effect: colloidal particles 1-1000 nm, comparable to wavelength, scattering less wavelength-dependent (white beam). A wrong answer equating the two shows failure to distinguish molecular vs. colloidal scattering regimes.

questions.q: A teacher claims: "If a liquid looks clear and colourless, it cannot be a colloid." Evaluate this statement using the Tyndall effect as evidence.
questions.a: The statement is false. Many colloids (e.g., dilute gelatin, some sols) appear clear and colourless to the naked eye but show a visible Tyndall beam when a laser passes through. The Tyndall effect is a more reliable diagnostic than visual clarity. A wrong answer agreeing with the teacher reveals the misconception that colloids must always look cloudy or opaque.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using household materials to test whether a given sample of "honey" is a true solution or a colloid. List materials, procedure, observation, and conclusion criteria.
questions.a: Materials: laser pointer, clear glass, water, honey sample. Procedure: Dilute honey in water (1:10), stir. Shine laser through the mixture in a dark room. Observation: If beam path is visible (bright cone), it's a colloid; if invisible, true solution. Criteria: Colloidal particles in honey (pollen, proteins) scatter light. A poor answer (e.g., "taste it" or "check if it dissolves") shows inability to apply the Tyndall effect as a diagnostic tool.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Tyndall effect is the ______ of a beam of light by colloidal particles (1 nm – 1000 nm) dispersed in a medium, making the light path visible as a bright cone.
Fill in the blank: Start with a real-world ______: in a dusty room or during a foggy morning in Delhi, a beam of sunlight entering through a window becomes visible as a bright path.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain why the Tyndall effect is observed in colloids but not in true solutions or suspensions, and can use it as a diagnostic test to distinguish colloids from true solutions in a given sample.
